why: the shape of a statement — what an engine accepts, what it values, and where a declaration is only a recommendation — pinned by execution rather than documentation.
from: FR-2 (mgmt-pg), as contributed; case format fixed and checks added before landing
appliesTo: every engine entry whose clock/types blocks are present, plus every entry in bindings
format: See verification/fixtures/README.md. Three additions were made while landing this set: `requires` can assert a capability is ABSENT (so a case can describe an engine that lacks it), `expects: "reject"` lets a case pin a refusal, and `check` makes the assertion machine-readable. The `assert` prose carries cross-engine truth the runner cannot reach.
checkScope: `check` is asserted on the engines this runner can reach (sqlite always, turso when its driver is installed). Postgres is skipped — this runner is dependency-free — so its shape is documented in `assert` and verified by verification/live/postgres.sql.
schema: CREATE TABLE t (id {identity.ddl}, name TEXT, active {types.map.boolean}, expires_at {types.map.timestamptz}, doc {types.map.jsonb})

cases.why: a bound LIMIT/OFFSET slot is a BINDING fact: the statement carries {ph}, which the runner renders from this binding's `params` style
steps: SELECT 1 AS v LIMIT {ph} OFFSET {ph}
assert: the engine accepts bound parameters in LIMIT/OFFSET slots

cases.why: guarded to the TEXT shape so the case is runnable without a pg driver. The postgres shape is the other half: timestamp with time zone, microseconds, tz-aware.
steps: SELECT {clock.serverNow} AS v, typeof({clock.serverNow}) AS ty
assert: the value is TEXT with second precision and no timezone — no subsecond, no offset
postgres returns a native timestamp with time zone at microsecond precision instead

cases.why: `<=` rather than `>` keeps the case deterministic across precisions: the stored value was taken before the query's own now.
steps: INSERT INTO t (id, expires_at) VALUES (1, {clock.serverNow})
SELECT id FROM t WHERE expires_at <= {clock.serverNow}
assert: the stored value and the query's now are comparable under the declared valueType

steps: CREATE TABLE ts (id {identity.ddl}, at {types.map.timestamptz} NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
INSERT INTO ts (id) VALUES (1)
SELECT at FROM ts WHERE id = 1
assert: DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is the portable suffix — measured true on all three
cases.why: CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is the portable default suffix; the case pins that the declared clock.ddlDefault form is accepted and evaluates, not merely written down.

steps: CREATE TABLE ts (id {identity.ddl}, at {types.map.timestamptz} NOT NULL DEFAULT now())
assert: DEFAULT now() is accepted — postgres only
cases.why: now() is the form that looks portable and is not — postgres accepts it, the SQLite family does not. The sibling rejection case needs this half.
the ABSENT half. `equals: false` is what makes it run on exactly the engines that declare ddlDefaultNow false; requiring the capability instead would SKIP there and assert nothing.
steps: CREATE TABLE ts (id {identity.ddl}, at {types.map.timestamptz} NOT NULL DEFAULT now())
assert: the DDL is refused — DEFAULT now() is a syntax error where ddlDefaultNow is false

steps: INSERT INTO t (id, active) VALUES (1, TRUE)
SELECT active FROM t WHERE id = 1
assert: the value round-trips as a real BOOLEAN on an enforcing engine
cases.why: on an engine that enforces types a boolean must come back a boolean — the value, not the declaration.

steps: INSERT INTO t (id, active) VALUES (1, TRUE)
SELECT active, typeof(active) AS ty FROM t
assert: active reads 1 with typeof 'integer' — affinity, not a boolean type (measured on sqlite and turso)
cases.why: on an unenforced engine the declared type is a recommendation: this pins what the value actually does (affinity to integer) so the DDL is not read as a constraint.
fail-closed does NOT apply where types.enforced is false, and this case proves the contract says so instead of pretending otherwise.
steps: CREATE TABLE z (a FLOOBLE)
assert: the DDL is accepted — affinity takes any type name, so there is nothing to refuse

steps: INSERT INTO t (id, doc) VALUES (1, '{"a":1}')
SELECT doc ->> 'a' AS v FROM t
assert: ->> works on ALL THREE, including the embedded engines (SQLite 3.38+)
cases.why: ->> is the extraction form that works on all three, including the embedded engines from SQLite 3.38; the case keeps that claim measured instead of assumed.

steps: INSERT INTO t (id, doc) VALUES (1, '{"a":1}')
SELECT doc @> '{"a":1}' AS v FROM t
cases.why: @> is accepted only by a native jsonb engine, so the case is gated on the declared map and the embedded engines do not run it.
the operator surface is where jsonb actually differs, not extraction. Asserting this keeps the difference from being over-stated in the other direction.
steps: INSERT INTO t (id, doc) VALUES (1, '{"a":1}')
SELECT doc @> '{"a":1}' AS v FROM t
assert: @> is refused at prepare time on the embedded engines

Measured 2026-10-22: sqlite reports unrecognized token for the @ character, turso reports a Parse error about array features. The pattern is deliberately a CLASS (parse-level rejection), because the wording is engine-version specific - this case was skipped until the driver was installed, and the drift was invisible until then.

cases.why: binding-scoped: the affected-row and insert-id field NAMES come from bindings.<name>.result, never from the engine entry
steps: INSERT INTO t (id, name) VALUES (1, 'a')
assert: the driver result carries the field named by result.affectedField
when result.insertIdField is null (pg), an id must come back via RETURNING instead

steps: SELECT 1 AS {identifierQuote}weird name{identifierQuote}
assert: the quoted identifier round-trips; a renderer emits only the declared quote, never sqlite's legacy backtick or bracket forms
cases.why: a name containing the quote character round-trips only if the renderer doubles it — the difference between quoting an identifier and concatenating one.

steps: {serverInfo}
assert: the declared query returns a version-shaped value
cases.why: the version statement is a per-engine fact; the case pins that the declared statement runs and returns a row rather than trusting the table.

runnerObligation: Same as tx.json — a fresh database per case, and `requires` checked FIRST so a capability the engine lacks is SKIPPED, never failed. Additionally: resolve {ph} and every binding-scoped case against the `bindings` section, never against the engine; and honour `expects: 'reject'` by asserting the refusal rather than letting the error escape.
